Earl Byrhtnoth and his thegns led the English against a Viking invasion . The battle <e1 ended> in an Anglo-Saxon defeat . After the battle Archbishop Sigeric of Canterbury and the aldermen of the south-western provinces <e2 advised> King Æthelred to buy off the Vikings rather than continue the armed <e3 struggle> . The result was a payment of 10,000 Roman pounds ( 3,300 kg ) of silver , the first example of Danegeld in England . An account of the battle , embellished with many speeches attributed to the warriors and with other details , is related in an Old English poem which is usually <e4 named> `` The Battle of Maldon '' . A modern embroidery <e5 created> for the millennium celebration in 1991 and , in part , depicting the battle , can be <e6 seen> at the Maeldune Centre in Maldon . one manuscript of the `` anglo-saxon chronicle '' states that a certain olaf , possibly the norwegian olaf tryggvason , <e7 led> the viking forces , these estimated to have been between 2,000 and 4,000 fighting men . A source from the 12th century , , written by the monks at Ely , <e8 suggests> that Byrhtnoth had only a few men to command : `` he was neither shaken by the small number of his men , nor fearful of the multitude of the enemy '' . Not all sources <e9 indicate> such a disparity in numbers . The poem `` The Battle of Maldon '' . `` The Battle of Maldon '' is the name conventionally <e10 given> to a surviving 325-line fragment of Old English poetry . Linguistic study has <e11 led to> the conjecture that initially the complete poem was <e12 transmitted> orally , then in a lost manuscript in the East Saxon dialect and now <e13 survives> as a fragment in the West Saxon form , possibly that of a scribe active at the Monastery of Worcester late in the 11th century . It is fortuitous that this was <e14 attached> at an early date to a very notable manuscript , Asser 's `` Life of King Alfred '' , which undoubtedly <e15 assisted> in its survival . the manuscript , by now detached , was <e16 burned> in the cotton library fire at ashburnham house in 1731 . Some <e22 favoured> <e23 paying> off the Viking invaders with land and wealth , while others <e24 favoured> <e25 fighting> to the last man . The poem <e26 suggests> that Byrhtnoth <e27 held> this latter attitude , hence his moving speeches of patriotism . The Vikings <e28 sailed> up the Blackwater ( then <e29 called> the Panta ) , and Byrhtnoth called out his levy . The poem <e30 begins> with him <e31 ordering> his men to <e32 stand> and to <e33 hold> weapons . His troops , except for personal household guards , were local farmers and villagers of the Essex Fyrd militia .
